Proceedings of the 54th Annual Meeting 


The Fifty-Fourth Avtioal Meeting of the Young Men’s 
Christian Association was held on Tuesday evening, May 11th. 
At 6.30 o'clock the Board of Directors and Committee men sat 
down to tea in the gymnasium which was served by the Ladies 
Committee. 

At the close of the tea, Dr. Grenfell gave an address con- 
cerning his work among the fishermen of Labrador. 

The Annual Meeting assembled in the Lecture Hall at 8.15. 
Mr.J.W. Knox, Vice- President, occupied the chair in the absence 
of the President, Mr. Robert Munro, on account of illness. The 
Secretary read the Annual Report of the Board of Directors 

Mr. L. H. Packard, Treasurer, presented the Financial 
Statement of the Association. 

Mr. Geo. A. Barrat presented the Membership Report. 

The Reports of the following Departments were then 
presented by their Chairmen : 


Physical - - - - O.C. Holland 
Educational - - - S&S. P. Leet 
Social - - - - - J. K. McNutt 
Religious - - - - G.E. Williams 
Foreign - -  -°- - DD. W. Ross 
Summer Camp - - B.S. R. Watson 
Junior - - - - A. L. Paterson 
Ladies Auxiliary - C.K. Calhoun 
Employment - - -  F. A. Matthews 
Railroad - - - - I. P. McLennan 


Mr. Williams, Chairman of the Committee on Nomination, 
presented the following names as Directors for the following 
three years : 


John Kennedy Chas. Cushing 
R. H. Buchanan Robert Munro 
C. C. Holland W. M. Birks 


R. L. Charlton 
These gentlemen were unanimously elected Directors. 


It was unanimously resolved that a telegram expressing 
the sympathy of the Association towards his speedy recovery be 
sent to Mr. Robert Munro at Clifton Springs, New York. Also 
a similar telegram be sent to Mr. W. Clelland, Chairman of the 
Membership ‘Committee, who was also laid aside through ill 
health at Clifton Springs Sanitorium. 

The meeting then adjourned.

FIFTY-FOURTH 


Annual Report of the Board of Directors 


In submitting this Fifty-fourth Annual Report the Direct- 
ors would call attention to four important Association events 
which have occurred during the past year: 


Buffalo Convention 


Ist. The holding of the 50th anniversary of the Inter- 
national Committee at Buffalo in May last. This Convention 
settled difficult problems which agitated the Brotherhood, 
and marked a new era in the Association movement on this 
continent. 


Visitation im Australia and New Zealand 


2nd. The contribution to the work for young men which 
was made by the visitation of the Associations of Australia 
and New Zealand by our Secretary. We confidently believe 
that this will lead to an enlarged interest in the work for 
young men in the cities and towns of Australasia. 


Chas. S. Paterson for India 


3rd. The sending out of Mr. Charles S. Paterson from 
this Association as Secretary of the Boys Branch in Calcutta, 
India. This Association considers itself highly honored by 
having such a worthy representative on its staff. The year 
just closed has shown a remarkable development in the 
work for young men in foreign lands,. and particularly in 
the providential adaptation of the Association work to the 
Japanese Army in Manchuria, and the good results which 
have already followed. Its effect upon the Hast will be far- 
reaching. This Association was one of the first, and has 
continued to be among the foremost, in its support of 
work for young men in foreign lands. 


10 


Dominion Conference 


4th. The holding of the Dominion Conference in this city 
in April last. This Conference not only settled questions 
which were disturbing our Association horizon in Canada, 
but outlined a policy, as indicated by the following resolu- 
tions, which should lead to the greater development of the 
Association movement throughout the Dominion: 


1. Increased Canadian representation (7 or 9 members) 
on the International Committee. Such members to be active 
Association men who shall attend the meetings of the Inter- 
national Committee, particularly the annual one, when 
the plans of the Committee for the ensuing year are con- 
sidered and adopted. 

2. The Canadian members of the International Commit- 
tee to be formed into a Canadian section with headquarters 
at Montreal, which will have cognizance of all Association 
work in the Dominion, and shall recommend to the Inter- 
national Committee (preferably at a meeting set apart for 
this purpose each year) the general plan of extension and 
supervision for Canada. 

3. The International Committee as a whole shall then 
agree upon the plan for the extension and supervision of 
Association work in Canada, and how these plans shall be 
earried out, it being understood that so far as consistent with 
the best interests of the work, the carrying out of said 
plans shall be placed in the hands of the Canadian section. 

4. That this Conference appoint a Committee of five to 
advise with the present Canadian members of the Inter- 
national Committee in the selection of the new members to 
be appointed as the additional Canadian members of that 
Committee. 

5. That the Canadian members of the International Com- 
mittee shall be considered the Dominion Committee, and shall 
be authorized to call another Dominion Conference whenever 
in their judgment advisable, after consultation with the 
International Convention or the International Committee. 


Membership 


The membership is ever the thermometer of our Associa- 
tion. On May Ist, after all expirations were deducted, the 
total number of members was 2367, an increase of 186 over 
last year. 709 joined,as new members, showing an average 
of about 60 applications for membership each month, or 
over two each day during the year. 


11 


Young men join the Association not alone for the material 
advantages afforded through the educational classes, gymna- 
sium and baths, the Reading Room and Library, but they 
come seeking good surroundings, congenial companion- 
ship, and to avoid the temptations which beset young 
men in city life. As a social and religious centre for 
young men this Association is becoming increasingly popular. 
The following extract from a letter recently received from 
a member who had removed to another city emphasizes the 
value of membership in the Association: 

‘*{ do not think I can adequately express to you, Mr. 
Budge, how much I miss the Association with all the true 
friends whom I met there, nor can I hope to enumerate the 
many blessings it brought into my life. I came from a 
small country-town in ’99, and my brother who had preceded 
me by one year, took me at once to the Association when I 
arrived. I feel that I owe almost all I have and am to it, and 
though far away I want to continue my membership 
in it. I know I am better physically, mentally, and best of 
all spiritually, through my connection with the Associa- 
tion, and I pray that it may continue to do for other young 
men what it has done for me, and for many of my chums. 
I cannot wish any young man better success than to become 
early interested in the three sides of this great movement 
which is doing so much to uplift young men.’’ 


Evening Education 


In the Educational Department the opportunity for study 
in 19 subjects on Commercial, Mechanical, and Language lines 
has been afforded to our members. Results have been secured 
which will be far-reaching both on the members who have 
enrolled and on the commercial and industrial life of the 
city. 

The growing interest in Evening Classes, and the appre- 
ciation of the value of evening hours as representing in- 
creased capacity, is such as to.demand better facilities than 
we have to offer. A re-arrangement of this Building is a 
necessity as the long-delayed Annex should be proceeded with 
at once if we are to meet this most urgent need. With suit- 
able facilities double the enrolment could be secured. 


The Physical Opportunity 


The work in the Physical Department has only been limited 
by the floor space in the gymnasium, and the number of 


}2 


lockers. Classes were conducted in 14 grades, and in the total 
attendance upon classes there was a gain of 1339 over last 
year. Twenty-six class sessions each week were conducted 
with 725 different men enrolled. There are 12 Athletic Clubs 
with a membership of over 500. 

Here also: there is need for enlarged accommodation. 
Arrangements are now being made which will give 200 addi- 
tional lockers for July 1st, but added Gymnasium floor space 
and enlarged Bowling Alleys are needed if we would meet 
the demand. 


The Social Life 


The social opportunity of the Young Men’s Christian 
Association is one of its greatest factors in reaching young 
men. Modern buildings are constructed with this feature 
largely in evidence, and the Association of the future will 
magnify its social work in all departments. 

This has been emphasized during the past year in the 
various clubs, seventeen of which are connected with the 
various departments. The Courses of Entertainments and 
Receptions have been most helpful to this end. The Strangers’ 
Tea on Sunday evenings has been a valuable factor, and the 
groups of Committees in their business meetings have largely 
developed the social spirit. The outings at the Summer 
Camp at Lac St. Joseph have made a definite contribution 
to the social side of our work. In outlining the work for 
next season each department should carefully consider this 
important feature in order to secure the best results. 


The Religious Life 


The Religious work really permeates the whole. It is not 
expressed only in the religious meetings and Bible classes, 
but in the Physical, Employment, Educational and in every 
department, the religious opportunity which the Associa- 
tion offers in its contact with men and boys, is one of the 
greatest which can possibly be desired. It is distinctly a 
‘* personal ’’ rather than a ‘‘ platform ”’ opportunity, and 
just in such measure as our employed officers and active 
workers realize the value of this unequalled vantage ground 
will larger results be secured. 

Three religious meetings for men and boys and fourteen 
classes for Bible Study: have been conducted during the past 
season with results which cannot easily be tabulated. EHighty- 


15 


one young men and boys have been introduced by letter to 
Pastors of city churches. 

The aim of the Association is to lead men to make a de- 
finite decision for the Christian life, and then to relate each 
man to some class for Bible Study and wherever possible to 
get him committed to some phase of Christian activity. 
Only in this way will his development and future usefulness 
be conserved. 


The Work for Boys 


The Boys work has been progressive and hopeful. The 
adding of the Intermediate Department and raising the age 
limit to 18 has been satisfactory. With this addition the 
membership is now 464, double that of last year. All the 
branches of this work show a gratifying increase, particularly 
the Bible Study, with a class enrolment of 170. 

In this department all the branches of the Association 
work—the Physical, Edueational, Social, and Religious—- 
are carried on. ‘To secure the best results there should be a 
separate equipment. The Association of the future will plan 
its Building with that in view. This is undoubtedly the great 
opportunity before the Association, because ‘‘ prevention ”’ 
is so much more economical, and productive of so much 
larger results, than ‘‘reformation.’’ Reach the boys and the 
men will be comparatively easy to reach. 

The present opportunity should arouse us to action, and is 
an added reason for the immediate re-arrangement and exten- 
sion of the Building to meet the requirements of this work. 


Daily Use of the Building 


The daily use of the building by men is an important fac- 
tor. It is open every week day from 8 a.m. till 10 p.m., and 
on Sundays except during the hours of church service. On 
May 8th an exact count was made from 8 a.m. till 10 p.m., 
which indicated that 950 young men entered the building 
during those hours. As there are no evening classes at this 
season the number would be increased by one-third during the 
fall and winter months — making a daily average attendance 
of 1200 young men during these months. 


The Association Finances 


The financial administration of this large and varied work 
ealls for the closest supervision by the Finance Committee. 
The receipts for members fees were $8460.00, and the amount 
received from members in subscriptions was $3030, making the 


1-+ 


total contribution by the members $11,490. EHighty-eight 
members made contributions in excess of their membership 
fee. The amount contributed by 412 citizens was $4480.00. 
In view of this large and varied work, and the rapid growth 
of the city there should be a larger number of the citizens 
who would share in this work. Why? Because of its practical 
and direct bearing on the commercial and industrial interests 
of the city. A prominent business man said recently, ‘‘ Aid 
to the Young Men’s Christian Association is an investment. 
It is a contribution to citizenship. It gives the youth 
instruction, entertainment, and encouragement. Its ideals are 
uplifting and refining. I would say to my fellow-business 
men, give liberally of your means, and give unconditionally. 
To those who can I would say, give more than money, give 
yourself. ’’ 

To many Associations on this continent large gifts have 
been made during the year. These are necessary for the 
extension and enlargement of the work—also for endow- 
ment of its Educational, Library and other Departments. 


Gifts by Bequest 


Since 1896 this Association has received $18,500 by bequest 
from eleven donors. During the past year we have received 
two bequests. One from the Exeeutors of the late A. F. 
Gault, $900; and one from the Executors of the late Mrs. N. 
B. Corse of $90. 


The Needs of the Association 


This Association now requires $100,000 for the extension 
and remodelling of the Dominion Square Building, and 
$9000 for the debt on the Railroad Men’s Building, Point 
St. Charles; and at least $50,000 for Branches which are now 
urgently demanded in other sections of the city. 

The Directors are impelled to keep this statement of their 
needs before the citizens, and confidently look for the gifts 
which will enable them to go forward as the work demands 
and the circumstances warrant. 


College Association Building 


During the past three years the Railroad Building has been 
completed, and now the handsome College Association Build- 
ing will be open for work in September. We congratulate the 
College Association im seeuring such a fine building in so 
prominent a situation, and we are sure it will render a 
large service to the young men of MeGill University. 


ley 
The Ladies’ Committee 


The Ladies’ Auxiliary has placed the Association under 
added obligation for the very helpful service which they 
have rendered during the year. They have taken entire 
charge of the larger social functions, and have assisted with 
supplies for the Strangers’ Tea and other socials. They have 
also rendered most valuable assistance in the furnishings 
required in the Boys’ Rooms, the Parlors, and the Kitchen. 


The Staff 


The Association has suffered loss in changes in its staff. 
Mr. E. 8. Conklin left in November to take a position as 
Assistant in one of the Branches of the Brooklyn Associa- 
tion. Mr. H. Ballantyne left in January to take the position 
of Seeretary of the Central Department Building in Toronto, 
and Mr. C. M. Daggett left in May to take the Junior Secre- 
taryship of the St. Louis, Mo., Association. We wish these 
friends every success in the development of this work for 
young men on the continent. 

The Directors wish to bear testimony to the unselfish and 
faithful service which has been rendered to the Association 
by all the members of the staff during the year.

sustained by the death of the following members and sub- 
seribers :

Some Statistics of the Wear’s Work 


Membership 


No. of new members admitted, 709. Of these 176 were church. 
members. 

No. of members received by transfer from other Associations, 73. 

The average age of members joining was 24. : 

Total number on April 30th, 2,367, and including Railroad Branch, 
2,823. 


Physical 


Twenty-six classes held each week in the gymnasium. 
Total class attendance, 15,971. 

480 members received physical examination. 
Number of Physical Department Clubs, 12. 

725 members enrolled in classes. 


Educational 


Total enrolment in the Evening Educational classes, 811. 
19 courses of study. 

Total attendance at Evening Educational classes, 10,883. 
Teachers employed, 14. 


Religious 


93 religious meetings for men. 

Total attendance, 6,351. 

174 class sessions for Bible Study in seven classes. 

Total attendance, 4,917. 

81 young men introduced to pastors of churches by letter. 

Amount contributed by members for Foreign Work in India,. 
$1,995.72. > 

Number of members who contribute to Foreign Work Fund, 200. 

18 Entertainments, Receptions, and Lectures were given. Total. 
attendance, 5,850. 


Employment 


840 applications for employment registered. 
204 situations secured. 


Library 
820 different members have used circulating Library. 


7,729 books have been drawn. 

207 new books added. 

The average daily attendance at the Reading Room, 227. 

The daily average attendance at the Building for the summer 
months, 850; for the fall and winter months, 1,200.

Boys’ Work 


Number of members of the Boys’ Department from 12 to 16 years 
of age, 234; of the Intermediate Department from 16 to 18, 117%. 

Boys who attended the religious services, 300. 

170 boys attended eight Bible Classes. 

68 boys were enrolled in educational classes. 

11 boys united with the church. 


Finance 


$11,490 contributed by members towards the local work. 

58 miempers made a contribution to current expenses in addition 
to theix membership fees. 

$4,480 contributed by 412 business men and citizens toward the 
suppor: of the local work. 


Social 


26 special Sunday evening teas were held for stranger young men. 
Total attendance at the same, 340, 

159 men and boys spent their vacation at the Summer Camp at 
Lae St. Joseph last season. 


Militia Camp 


A well equipped Association tent was handled in the Militia Camp 
at Laprairie. 


Railroad Branch 


Number of members in Railroad Branch, 456. 

Meals and lunches served at the Railroad Branch, average 91 daily. 

Rest Rooms used by Railroad men, 13,856 times. 

Average daily attendance at the Railroad Department, 360. 

A Boarding House and Room Register is consulted by hundreds of 
men throughout the year. 


Membership 


The Membership Committee has carefully considered all matters 
relating to the membership. On November 12th, Mr. E. 8. Conklin, 
the Membership Secretary, removed to the Association at 26th Ward 
Branch, Brooklyn, N.Y. He is succeeded by Mr. P. A. Doig.

OV 


Religious 


The stated religious work of the Association so far as that is 
expressed in the weekly meetings and Bible Classes has been carried on 
regularly during the year. 

The Saturday Night Meeting shows a total attendance of 2,565, at 
52 meetings, average 49. 

Enquirers have been met with frequently, and several instances of 
decisions for Christ have greatly encouraged the members of the Com- 
mittee. The attendance has occasionally been small during the summer 
months, but the fall and winter season always shows returning strength. 
The meetings have been marked by spiritual helpfulness, especially 
during the last six weeks. 

The Men’s Meeting on Sunday afternoon was held from October 
to April, and met at three o’clock instead of four as formerly. Thirty- 
one meetings were held, with a total attendance of 3,786, average 122. 
This is a decrease over last year of 117. The Committee account for 
this in three ways: J irst, to a slight extent, the change in the hour; 
second, our inability to get as large a number of strong outside speakers 
as in the previous year; third, failure to effect as large an organization 
of workers as a service of this kind demands. 

The meetings proved to be of exceedingly high order, and on several 
occasions deep, spiritual impression was noticeable, and encouraging 
evangelistic results secured. Special mention should be made of the 
meetings addressed by Mr. E. W. Booth, of New York; Mr. F. 8. 
Brockmam, of Shanghai, China; Mr. Geo. G. Mahy, of Scranton, Pa.; 
Mr. A. G. Knebel, of New York; Rev. Bradford Williams, vf Brooklyn, 
N.Y.; Mr. Galen M. Tisher, of Tokio, Japan; and Rev. T. 8S. MeWil- 
liams, D.D., of Cleveland, Ohio. The kind assistance of these gentlemen 
was supplemented by able addresses from several of our own city pas- 
tors, to all of whom our hearty thanks are due. 

The musical service was under the leadership of Mr. Cecil M. 
Daggett, assisted by Messrs. Geo. Best, O. B. Keddy, and F. D. Carter, 
who formed with Mr. Daggett the Male Quartette, which greatly added 
to the attractiveness and value of the meetings. On several occasions 
solos were rendered by other friends, to whom we are very glad to 
express our thanks. 

The Sunday Afternoon Bible Class had a total attendance of 3,048, 
being an average attendance of 59 for 51 Sundays on which the class 
regularly met. The average at the class shows a decrease of seven for 
the year, which is, no doubt, due to the change in the hour for the fall 
and winter season. The average attendance during the months from 
May to September was 74, and from October to April, 47. Notwith- 
standing, good work was accomplished, and the class has filled a place 
of large usefulness in the Association. The following gentlemen have 
conducted or addressed the class on occasion: Mr. F. W. C. Meyers, 
Mr. H. Ballantyne, Mr. Morgan, of London, England; Rev. Dr. Smith, 
of St. Catherines; Mr. E. T. Colton, of New York; and Mr. H. J. Keith, 
now of Calcutta. 

A departure was made this year in haying the Sunday Afternoon 
Bible Class and the Gymnasium Men’s Bible Study Club meet for tea 
on Sunday evening at 5.30 after the class session, uniting with the 
Strangers’ Tea in the use of the hour. This was one of the most interest- 
ing gatherings in the Association, usually about 60 or 70 men being 


26 


present. The expense of the Committee was largely defrayed by 
voluntary contributions. Atter tea a half-hour ot sacred song with 
remarks by occasional visitors gave a devotional value to the occasion. 

The Social Song Service on Sunday evening after church was con- 
ducted throughout the winter months under the leadership of the 
Secretaries who took turns in presiding. ‘l’his gathering was very infor- 
mal in character, and served to make a profitable rallying place for 
men after the evening church services. 

The week-night Bible Classes were organized on October 4th, and 
continued throughout the fall and winter on Tuesday evenings from 
seven to eight o’clock. For the convenience of the students tea was 
served at 6.30 previous to the class, which did much to promote good 
feeling and mutual acquaintance. ‘The thanks of the Association are 
due Rey. J. L. Gilmour and Messrs. F. W. C. Meyers and Geo. E. Wil- 
liams, who so acceptably conducted classes. 

The names of 81 men and boys were sent to pastors during the year 
in reference to visitation and church membership. 

Visitation of the Western Hospital on Sunday mornings has been 
conducted under the leadership of Messrs. W. 8. Leslie and T. M. 
Barrington, assisted by other friends. A brief devotional service is held 
in the different wards, which we believe is appreciated by the patients. 

Visitation of sick young men has been made in the other hospitals 
of the city as occasion offered. The kindness of our Ladies’ Commit- 
tee has enabled us to send flowers to sick young men from time to time. 

The Association tent was placed in the Militia Camp at Laprairie, 
June 28th to July 8th, and work conducted there for the men in co- 
operation with the Provincial Committee for Ontario and Quebec. Mr. 
Artnur F. Bell was in charge, assisted by Mr. W. 8. Hopkins, of Sher- 
brooke. The tent was largely patronized by the men during the day and 
evening. Words of commendation from both officers and men assure us 
of its great usefulness, 

The attendance at the meetings and Bible Classes for the year was 
as follows:—

foreign Work 


The past year has been an eventful one, inasmuch as our own repre- 
sentative in the Foreign Field, Mr. Chas. 8. Paterson, left us in Septem- 
ber for his field of labor amongst the boys of Caleutta. ‘The reports 
from him are most encouraging as to the scope and opportunity for work 
amongst the boys of India. 

We have derived great inspiration from the visits and addresses 
of Mr. John R. Mott, Mr. F. S. Brockman, of China, and Mr. Galen oM. 
Fisher, of Japan, representatives of the International Committee in 
those countries. 

Our supporting membership now numbers 197, and the Committee 
are planning for a systematic effort to increase this largely, encourag- 
ing the contribution of the smallest sums as the means of educating a 
large percentage of our membership to systematic giving to the support 
of work in Foreign Lands. As one has lately well said :— 

“* No expression of the depth of the religious life of a Y.M.O.A. 
is so complete as the one to be found in that growing extension of its 
activities by which out beyond the immediate Building, farther than the 
limits of the Municipality whose name it bears, to lands and peoples they 
never have seen, the work is carried.’’ 

The stirring incident of late has been the access given to the work 
of the Association amongst iue Japanese Army, and the marvellous 
acceptance and acknowledgment of its benefits, by the Emperor of Japan 
and the highest officials, whilst from the soldiers themselves the most 
touching and pathetic accounts are received of their gratitude. 

The Committee was so impressed with this opportunity for service 
that a sum of $200.00 was promised towards its support, $100.00 of 
which has been remitted from the funds of the Committee, and $100.00 
remains to be contributed. Not a member of our Association can afford 
to do without some share in this blessed work. 

Amongst the Juniors great interest has been developed, and a very 
considerable sum of money raised by themselves for Mission Work, which 
will be reported upon more fully in the Report of the Junior Department. 

Our Financial Statement from October 1, 1903, to April 30, 1905, 
is as follows: —

Lducational 


Evening Educational classes for senior members were conducted im 
sixteen subjects, commencing October 3rd, with a total attendance of 
10,014, compared with 8,993 last year, not including the spring term, 
figures tor which are not yet to hand. 

Classes were also conducted for junior members in Shorthand, 
Arithmetic, and Penmanship, with a total attendance of 896, compared 
with 778 last year. Total amount of tuition fees received was $1,665.05, 
compared with $1,402 last year. 

The work this year was divided into fall, winter, and spring terms, 
commenced respectively on October 3rd, January 9th, and April 3rd. 
The spring term included classes in Shorthand, Mechanical Drawing, 
French, and German only. 

Eighty-four men (the same number as last year) wrote on the 
International Examinations in six subjects. Forty-five (three more than 
last year) passed the local examiners, and their papers were forwarded 
to the International Examiners in New York for final marking. 

The details of the classes for the fall and winter terms are as 
follows :—

present.

Atlantic Steam Navigation,’’ by Mr. Geo. Hannah; 60) 
present. 

Mar. 14.—‘‘Salesmanship,’’ by Mr. Jas. A. Ogilvy, Jr.; 65 present. 

Mar. 21—‘‘Tllustrated Travel Talk on Australia,’’? by Mr. D. A. Budge; 
400 present.

We regretted, just at the beginning of the second term, to lose the 
services of Mr. Ballantyne, and we wish here to recognize his faithful 
work during his stay among us. 

The increased efficiency of this department is largely due to his 
energy, tact, and good comradeship. 

We believe this department is capable of very much more than it 
has yet done for the young men ot our city whose early opportunities 
to get an education have been limited. 


Ss. P. LEET, Chairman. 


Social 


The desired tendency in the Association is to make the social spirit 
to prevail among us, especially in good comradeship and healthy enjoy- 
ment in all our many-sided activities. There are many social features 
which do not fall directly under the care of this Committee, but which 
are touched upon in reports from the other departments. 

With the exeeption of a social gathering in September for new 
members who had joined during the summer, the efforts of the Com- 
mittee this year were directed toward making the Entertainment Course 
a success. Although not as well patronized by the members as expected, 
we believe that these entertainments filled a place in the Association, 
and we look for better things next season. The expenses of the course 
were $575.83, and the receipts $405.03, leaving a deficit of $170.80. 


The dates and talent were as follows:— 


Tuesday, Oct. 25.—Fred. Emerson Brooks, of Boston, Poet-Humorist. 

Tuesday, Noy. 15.—John Thomas Concert Co., of Boston. 

Thursday, Dec. 15.—Association Glee Club, and Pitt Parker, Crayon 
Artist, of Philadelphia. 

Monday, Jan. 2.—Annual New Year’s Concert, by the Alexis Concert 


Co. 

Thursday, Jan. 26—E. S. Williamson, Toronto. Illustrated Lecture: 
‘*Pickwick Papers.’’ 

Thursday, Feb. 23.—Wesleyan Male Quartette, and Miss Jackson, of 
Chicago. 

Monday, Mar. 6.—Rey. Thos. McClary, Lecture, ‘‘The Mission of 
Mirth.’’ 

Thursday, Mar. 23.—Frank Yeigh, Toronto, Picture Travel Talk: 

: ‘Britain and Brittany.’’ 


Thanksgiving Day was pleasantly observed by an evening dinner, 
in which 80 young men participated. Instead of giving this dinner by 
invitation, as formerly, the Committee placed the tickets at 25 cents 
each, and freely invited members and young men who were away from 
home on that day to attend. The results were much better than under 
the old plan. After dinner a programme of songs and speeches was 
carried out. The Ladies’ Committee assisted us in their usual whole- 
hearted way. 


31 


The Annual New Year’s Day Reception was duly arranged for and 
passed off quite as successfully as in former years, which is saying all 
that can be said. This occasion is entered into so heartily by the entire 
Association Membership and friends, and the success of past years ‘has 
been so great that it becomes difficult to vary the proceedings materially 
or to add in any measure to the enjoyment of the day. It was the 
opinion of the Board of Directors and the Committee that a large 
number were present than in any previous year. Members of the Board, 
assisted by members of the Committee, were in constant attendance on 
the Reception Floor to receive our guests. The usual gymnasium pro- 
gramme was carried out, a most attractive feature being a fencing 
exhibition between two of our Japanese members. 

An illustrated lecture by Mr. C. T. Williams, on ‘‘A World Wide 
View of the Association,’’ was well received, The Ladies’ Committee 
served refreshments during the afternoon. In the evening Mr. G. R. 
Lighthall gave a very interesting illustrated lecture on ‘‘ Holland,’’ and 
the evening concert by the Alexis Co., of Boston, was a pronounced 
success, 

We were indebted to many friends, who kindly loaned us pictures 
and other articles for the day. 

The Sunday Afternoon Strangers’ Tea was served fortnightly during 
the summer months, and enabled us to help many strange young men 
who came to the city at that time of the year. Commencing in October 
the Strangers’ Tea combined with the Bible Class on Sunday afternoon 
so that for more than half of the year it was served at the Building 
each Sunday afternoon. This formed a valuable adjunct to the Reli- 
gious work as well as to the Social. Thus the Strangers’ Tea was not so 
distinctive as formerly, but a thorough social gathering replaced it 
which could not but be inspiring to officers and strangers. It also 
served to bring our members into healthful acquaintance with strangers. 

The Chess Club was organized early in the season with a member- 
ship of about 25. Good interest has been observed in the games and 
tournaments throughout the year. : 

The Orchestra rehearsed regularly during part of the fall and win- 
ter, and rendered important assistance, particularly at New Year’s. 

The Reception Committee was re-organized during the year, and 
under the chairmanship of Mr. J. B. Sellars has continued to render 
important service in the office and on the reception floor on week 
evenings. 

The Glee Club had a successful season under the leadership of Mr. 
C. M. Daggett as Musical Director. 

In addition to taking part in the Association Entertainment Course 
the Club assisted at several social gatherings, bringing their season to 
a close with a most enjoyable ‘‘at home’’ in the Association parlors on 
April 24th. 

The Committee have carefully considered the work of the past 
season, and have already recommended new plans to the Board of Direc- 
tors, which we trust will receive attention early in the coming year. 


JAMES K. MeNUTT, Chairman. 


32 
Essociation Glee Club 


This Club can report, for the season just past, one of the most 
successful and prosperous years in its history. It has not only been 
a source of enjoyment and help to each member, but the singing of the 
Club was also very much appreciated by the different audiences they 
sang to. 

This Club is self-supporting, covering this year, all the ordinary 
expenses required to run the Club. 

Great credit is due to Mr. Daggett, the leader of the Club, for the 
high standard of efficiency it has reached.

Pbysical 


We live in a time of muscle-saving devices, and as a result during 
the past thirty years muscular effort has decreased eighty per cent. on 
this continent. Under the conditions of city life to-day exercise is 
becoming as necessary to keep the body healthy as food and water are to 
nourish it. Exercise is the life of a muscle, without which it dies. Not 
only does city life make less demand upon the muscular system, but it 
increases the work of the nervous system. The importance of exercise 
as offered in the Association Gymnasium is thus emphasized :— 

The Young Men’s Christian Association on this continent conduct 
556 gymnasiums, with 135,000 men and boys taking regular systematic 
exercise under the leadership of 365 Physical Directors. 

‘*Outing’’ in a recent editorial stated that ‘‘the Association in 
point of honest fact is doing more practical good with its athletics 
than all the Colleges and Athletic Clubs combined.’’ It is now 
admitted by competent observers that the Association has become the 
leading factor in physical training, clean sport, and healthful recreation 
in North America. 


33 


A review of our work for the past year shows marked progress. 
Gymnasium classes were conducted for thirteen different grades of our 
membership, ranging from 12 to 50 years of age. In the interests of these 
different groups 747 class sessions were held, with a total attendance 
of 15,971, an average of over 2,200 per month, and a gain of 1,339 in 
gross attendance over last year. There were 725 names registered in 
the twenty-six weekly classes, with attendance as follows:—

480 men were physically or medically examined. The twelve athletic 
-clubs which are an integral feature of the department have a mem- 
bership of over 500. About 1,200 different members use the department. 

The formation of an intermediate class for business boys has been 
in every way helpful. Not only did it relieve the over crowded elemen- 
tary class. but it grouped together those with a common interest, and 
thereby made for itself a real place among the other classses. The 
-elementary class shows a consequent decrease in attendance, but there 
is a net gain to the department through the change. 

Through the kindness of Dr. H. B. Cushing a course of lectures 
in ‘‘ First Aid to the Injured’’ was provided, with an average attendance 
of 30. 

The Committee desire to record their sincere appreciation of the 
invaluable service rendered by Dr. W. F. Gilday and Dr. H. B. Cushing 
as medical examiners. Mr, H. M. Peacock has rendered valuable ser- 
vice as gymnasium instructor in the Fairmount Young Men’s Associa- 
tion. Mr. Geo. E. Winter, one of our oldest members, was obliged to 
resign on account of leaving the city. Mr. A. G. Burton and Mr. L. A. 
Wilkinson were elected as new leaders. 

The Annual Banquet held on Mareh 2nd was an enjoyable function. 

The New Year’s Reception and the Physical Department Banquet 
on April 27th both passed off successfully. 


Harrier Club 


This Club won the City Championship in the fall of 1903. They 
had an average attendance at all their spring runs of 20, and the Club 
membership is 42. 

On May 12th, at the invitation of Mr. Geo. Palmer, they held a 
paper chase in Montreal South, which was the best of the season’s 
-outings. 


b+ 


As the want of a Harrier’s Association or League was beginning: 
to be felt in the city, the club, together with the M.A.A.A. took the 
initiative in forming what is now known as the Montreal District Har- 
rier League, the governing body of cross country and long distance 
running in and around Montreal. A programme for the spring, which 
included several Union Runs, two Team Races, and a Track Meet, was 
drawn up by the League, and in all of these our Club took a leading: 
part. In the team races, which. were held for Seniors and Juniors on 
May 14th and 21st respectively, they came out first, winning both by a 
good margin, and so adding two more silver cups to that won the pre- 
vious fall, which was for the ‘‘Louis Rubenstein Cup.’’ In the Senior 
Race, out of six teams, comprising 36 runners, our team finished 2nd, 
3rd, 5th, 11th, and 13th. In the Junior Race for a trophy presented 
by the Montreal District Harrier League, out of five teams, comprising: 
30 starters, our team secured 3rd, 5th, 7th, 10th, and 14th place. 
Silver Association stick pins were given to the members of both teams: 
as souvenirs. 

At the Track Meet, held by the Harrier League, on May 28th, they 
secured Ist in the One Mile, 2nd in the Two Mile, 3rd in the 100 Yards,, 
Half-Mile, Two Mile Junior, and Five Mile. 

The last event of the season was the Team Road Race, conducted 
by the Grand Trunk Boating Club, held on Saturday, November 12th,, 
on the Lower Lachine Road. The Grand Trunk Boating Club put up 
a team trophy and three individual cups for the Ist, 2nd, and 3rd 
places, and our club took the best three of the four. Out of 24 starters 
our team secured Ist, 2nd, 6th, 10th, and 11th places. 

At the Annual Association Field Day, the ‘‘W. S. Leslie Cup’” 
was again competed for, and was won by the team captained by Mr. 
Fred. Smith. 

Through the kindness of Mr. W. S. Leslie, our Honorary-President,, 
and several other gentlemen connected with the Association, it was 
possible to send a team to Toronto, and Messrs. Stanley, Palmer, Smith, 
and McCuaig were the men chosen to represent our Club. 


We close the season with an almost even financial balance. 


Bowling 


Opening our alleys on October first, we gave a gold spoon each 
week for the highest single string, and the scores made were very good. 
We formed a League with the Railroad Association, two teams from 
each club. Some of the scores made were over 3,100, in one match 11 
men out of 12 had over 500. The highest score for three strings in a’ 
match was 614. The highest team score was 3,174. 


The ‘‘Crescents’’ of our Association were fortunate in winning 
the Championship Cup, which was put up by the members and which 
now adorns the Association Cabinet. The ‘‘Maples,’’ also of our 
Association, came second. 

After the League matches closed, the Committee arranged a new 
competition for the highest average for ten strings made during six 
weeks, giving three prizes. This competition is now in progress, and 
the interest taken is very keen. One of the members has an average 
of 236, and is followed by three others. 

During the season wé sold 5,142 tickets, which is a large increase: 
over other years.

This Club regrets that it cannot present a more satisfactory report. 
Failing to secure the Arena as formerly, it could only engage the 
Prince Arthur Rink two nights per week from seven to eight, and this 
did not suit our men. To help our expenses several games of basket- 
ball were arranged for, the proceeds going to the funds of the club. A 
team was entered in the Junior League, but through various causes, did 
not finish the schedule. Of the three matches played the club won two. 
Unless proper ice can be had for another season, it is a question if it 
is wise to continue the club. 


BasKetbali 


Four teams were entered in the senior league, and four in the 
intermediate, representing 64 players. The teams were very evenly 
matched, and the spirit of the players was good. The umpiring was 
done by Mr. Merritt, assisted by different players, and helped to make 
the game cleaner and faster. The ‘‘Maples’’ won the senior cham- 
pionship, captained by Mr. A. E, Smaill, and the ‘‘Tigers’’ won the 
intermediate. A representative team was picked to play for the city 
championship, and made a creditable showing, winning all the home 
games and losing the three outside games, by a total of four points. 

Outside teams played in our gymnasium from Quebee, Peter- 
borough, McGill, Railroad Y.M.C.A., and Westmount. 


The Association Snowshoe Club 


36 


Baseball 


The past season, however, was attended by events which may be: 
remembered with thankfulness, as well as others which have left a sense 
of regret. Through the kindness of the Montreal Eastern League Club, 
we were fortunate in securing the use of their grounds. Membership 
29, last year 18. Practices were well attended. 


Snowshoe 


This Club reports the most successful season in its history. The ° 
membership has increased six per cent. over last year, and with 33 1-3 
per cent. more outings. 

The Annual Reception was held on December 8th, with 150 of the 
members and their friends. We have held 14 tramps and two sleigh 
drives, with an average attendance of 33. Of the tramps five have been 
ladies’ tramps, eight for men only, and one Union Tramp. 

Three of the members entered for the races held by the ‘‘ Holly’’ 
and ‘‘Montagnard’’ Clubs. In the ‘‘Montagnard’’ Club races our men 
took 3rd and 4th places in the three mile open. 

Our membership shows a total of 76. 


Tennis 

The past year has been the most successful in the whole history of 
the Club. There was an average attendance each evening of not less 
than 15. Membership 33. A credit balance of $10.13. 


Football and Athletic Club 


A number of the members of the Athletic Club decided to form a 
Football Club, and a membership of 30 men was secured. They had a 
good season’s record, and played several games in connection with the 
Montreal and District Intermediate League. 

In regard to athletics weekly handicaps were held on the track at 
the ball park, and those obtaining the highest percentage of wins in 
track and field events were presented with suitable prizes, at’ the close 
of the season. 

The Field Day was heid on the M.A.A.A. grounds in September. 
There were over sixty entries, the events were well contested and run 
off on schedule time. New features were an obstacle race and a, two 
mile walking race. 


Bible Study Club 


The Gymnasium Men’s Bible Study Club’’ continues to be a 
prominent factor in the social and moral life of the department. 
Studies in ‘‘Life Principles’? have been most helpful. The total 
attendance for the year was 1,157, with an average of 35. The Club 
held thirty-three sessions and enrolled 77 different men. 


Cc. C. HOLLAND, Chairman.

From these figures it will be seen that the addition of the Inter- 
mediate Department for boys 16-18 years of age, has greatly added to 
our membership, and that at the present time we are conducting work 
for twice as many boys as we were May 1, 1904. 


Religious 

The Friday Evening Meeting has been held regularly throughout. 
the year with the exception of the months of July and August. All our 
efforts have been directed towards making this an older boys’ meeting. 
The average attendance for the year has been 35, as compared with 
44 last year. Two-thirds of the attendants at this meeting are business 
boys. 
The younger boys’ meeting has been continued as a Bible class on 
Wednesday afternoons, at the close of the gymnasium class, and has 
been conducted by the Secretary. The total enrolment of this class 
has been 90, average attendance 40. 

300 individual boys in our membership have been reached by these 
two meetings. 

Song Services have been conducted at the Montreal General Hos- 
pital every second Sunday morning from October to May. The average 
attendance for the year has been 30. Special services were conducted 
at Christmas and Easter. 

The following Bible Classes have been conducted in addition to the 
younger boys’ meeting mentioned above:—

During the year 58 boys have expressed a desire to enter the 
Christian life, and 11 have joined churches. 11 other boys are con- 
sidering the matter of church membership.

Summer Camp at Dac St. Joseph 


Senior Camp 


The Camp was open from the 16th July to the 6th September, and 
had an attendance of 80 men. This was a slight increase over last 
year, and while a number of the usual campers were missing, their 
places were filled by some of our newer members. The right kind of 
weather prevailed, and the fishing was good. Our annual Regatta and 
several mock trials were pleasing features in the Camp. ‘The gasoline 
launch, whue in working order, added much to the enjoyment of the 
campers. 

Mr. Harry Ballantyne, in charge from July 16th to 30th. 

Mr. Peter Doig, in charge from 30th July to 30th August. 

Mr. Alex. Ross, in charge from 30th August to 6th September. 

Services were held regularly every Sunday morning—generally by 
those in charge. Service of song in the evening. The Christian 
influence which the Camp easts around the lake is much appreciated 
by the residents, as is testified by the number attending these services. 
The Camp Committee is greatly indebted to Mr. Hadley for his kind- 
ness and generosity in presenting an organ to the Camp. 

After paying all running expenses for the season, there is a balance 
on hand of $33.20. 

Recommendations for next year:— 

Ist. Walls of ice-house be packed with sawdust, and proper venti- 
lation be made in roof, 

2nd. Permanent wharf. 

3rd. Mattresses of some sort to lay on the board floors of the 
tents. 


B.S. R. WATSON, Chairman Senior Camp Com,

The Association Islands, Lac St. Joseph. Club and Vacation Resort.

Junior Camp 


The Junior Executive Committee conducted its camp this season 
in two sections. The first for the Business Boys June 18th to July 
2nd, attendance 35, the second for the School Boys, July 2nd to July 
15th, attendance 44, total 79. This is the largest camp ever conducted 
by this Department. 

The Secretary was in charge, and the entire four weeks were spent 
in boating, swimming, fishing, etc. No accident or serious illness 
marred the pleasure of the camp life, and everybody returned to the 
city well browned and happy. 

The religious work carried on was particularly successful. The 
Boys’ Meetings on the Friday evenings, the Sunday services, the Bible 
class under the trees every morning, the prayers every evening in the 
tents, and the personal work of the leaders with each and every boy— 
all bore fruit in decisions for Christ. At the two camps sixteen boys 


expressed a desire to begin the Christian life. All these boys are now 
in Bible classes.

‘Railroad ADen’s Branch, Point St. Charles 


In presenting this, the first report for a full year in the new 
Building, we are glad to report progress in the different depart- 
ments of the work. The number of members now on the roll is 456; 
the largest number during the year was 630. The attendance at the 
rooms shows a daily average of 360, During the winter every part of 
the Building was kept full. The Reading Room is well supplied with 
magazines and papers. Five Educational Classes were carried on, with 
an attendance of 1,746. The Shorthand and Telegraphy Classes have 
continued for the summer term. The social atmosphere of the Building 
has been good, eleven socials and entertainments were held during the 
year, with an attendance of 1,089. The religious is represented by 
180 meetings held during the year, with an attendance of 8,092. A 
mixed meeting Sundays, with an average attendance of 150. A 
monthly men’s meeting, with an attendance of 90. Bible Classes on 
Saturday night and Sunday morning, and a Song Service Sunday after 
church, have been the regular meetings. 


42 


The use of the Rest Rooms has increased each month, 13,856 beds 
being used during the year. A number of regular roomers haye been 
taken lately. 

The bath rooms have been used 6,471 times during the year. 

The physical work has been carried on since September, 112 
classes have been held, and a suecessful basketball league formed. 
A baseball and a lacrosse team have been formed for the summer, 
and ‘he court fitted up for track events. The bowling alleys have 
been very popular, 7,698 tickets have been sold. 

In November Mr..F. L. Greer resigned as Secretary, and he was 
suceeeded by Mr. L. P. McLennan.

Ladies’ Buriliary 


The Ladies’ Auxiliary held eight meetings for conference over 
their work—with a larger average attendance than last year. 

In November a reception was tendered to Mr. and Mrs. Budge on 
their retufn from their trip to Australia and New Zealand, in which 
tue Auxiliary co-operated with the Association. At the December meet- 
ing Mrs. Budge gave an interesting account of her experience in the 
Auxiliary work in the places visited. 

The Social Committee, of which Miss Mabel Williams was con- 
vener, took charge of the refreshments at the following functions: 
The Committee Men’s Annual Tea, the Reception to Mr. and Mrs. Budge, 
the Thanksgiving Day Supper, the New Year’s Day Reception, the 
Physical Department Banquet, and other smaller social events. In 
addition to these, cake has been provided for the Strangers’ Tea, 
which is held fortnightly during the year. 

The Furnishing Committee, of which Mrs. Peter Laing was Con- 
vener, expended $104.38 in re-covering parlor furniture, adding a cozy 
corner, two oak seats, sofa pillows, etc., also seven table cloths and 
some glassware, and ten dozen cups. In view of proposed changes in 
the Building it was not deemed wise to spend more at present. There 
was also a grate placed in the parlor as a gift from Mrs. Geo. Hyde. 

The Flower Committee, Mrs. John McKergow, Convener, supplied 
the Building once each week with flowers, also for receptions, and sent 
flowers to young men who were sick either in hospitals, homes, or 
boarding houses, whose names were sent to them by the officers of the 
Association. In addition to the contribution of flowers from friends, 
the Committee expended $14.25. 

The Junior Committee, Mrs. John W. Ross as Convener, reports a 
membership of 19. They provided for six teas and eleven socials for 
the Boys’ Department during the year. An afternoon tea was given 
in January to the mothers of the boys when the work of the Depart- 
ment was explained. This was so much appreciated it should be 
repeated each year. Of the $30.00 voted to us by the Auxiliary, $25.00 
was spent in the purchase of a round table for the Boys’ Reading 
Room, curtains, ete. 

The young ladies of the Committee rendered most practical and 
helpful service. Miss Tees acted as Secretary of the Committee. 

The Finance Committee, Mrs. Busteed, Treasurer, reports 137 mem- 
bers who have paid their subscriptions, which is six less than last year.
